title: Understanding Israel’s Campaign to Destroy Palestinian Refugee Camps in the West Bank
summary: All 19 Palestinian refugee camps in the West Bank were created between 1948 and 1950 to house Palestinians who had been forcibly displaced from their homes in what became Israel proper during the Nakba. The UN Relief and…

body.section1: All 19 Palestinian refugee camps in the West Bank were created between 1948 and 1950 to house Palestinians who had been forcibly displaced from their homes in what became Israel proper during the Nakba. The UN Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) rented plots of land to establish the camps with 90-year contracts, making the UN the legal real estate rights holder in the camps, which were never expanded. For the masses of refugees who had lost everything, these camps became their only housing choice amid precarious living conditions, poverty, and overcrowdedness, to which the social stigma of being dispossessed was added.
body.section2: Over the years, resistance to Israel became a main feature of the collective identity of refugee camps, where Palestinians originating from different social backgrounds were forging new communities centered around the idea of dispossession and marginalization. Although it is the mass or armed groups’ resistance that made the West Bank refugee camps famous, it is something else that made the core of their identities, and which brewed conditions for a culture of resistance in the first place.

title: 2026 Paying for News is Cheaper Than Not Having It

body.heading1: The Internet Has Destroyed the Traditional Business Model of Journalism and Harmed the Public Interest
body.section1:
The article argues that journalism once thrived because newspapers relied on profitable local advertising monopolies. This revenue model allowed news organizations to employ large numbers of journalists who provided public oversight, investigated institutions, and helped maintain transparency in society. However, the rise of the internet shifted advertising revenue to major technology companies such as Google and Facebook, whose scale and targeting capabilities allowed them to dominate the market. As a result, newspapers lost their financial foundation, many news organizations collapsed, and thousands of journalists lost their jobs.

The author emphasizes that big technology companies benefited from the economic value of news without taking responsibility for producing journalism. Their primary business is capturing and selling user attention, not funding reporting. Social media platforms can generate large amounts of content from users at little cost, reducing the incentive to invest in professional journalism. This has created an environment where commentary and opinion are expanding while original reporting is shrinking, leaving citizens with less reliable information and weakening democratic accountability.
body.heading2: Journalism Should Be Treated as a Public Good Requiring New Support Models
body.section2:
The article argues that journalism faces a structural crisis rather than merely a problem of poor management. Like healthcare, transportation, and housing, journalism serves an important public function but cannot always be sustained by profit-driven markets alone. The author suggests that public funding may be necessary to ensure the continued existence of independent reporting and to protect society’s access to accurate information.

At the same time, the author believes journalism must develop new financial models suited to the digital era. Traditional “free” news was actually supported by advertising and users’ attention, but that model has collapsed. Independent journalists increasingly rely on subscriptions and direct support from readers, requiring the public to recognize that quality journalism has real costs. Building a culture of paying for journalism, combined with broader structural reforms, is presented as a long-term solution to preserving a healthy information ecosystem.
